content:
noirlab2629 — Photo Release

A crystal-clear image of the Betta Fish Nebula floating by countless stars makes a splash

23 November 2026

Wispy blue ribbons of stellar matter float deep in the cosmos, appearing like the waving tails of betta fish. This stunning snapshot features the best, most detailed view of supernova remnant SNR G295.5+09.7 to date. It was captured by the U.S. Department of Energy-fabricated Dark Energy Camera, mounted on the U.S. National Science Foundation Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile.

This wispy structure is the supernova remnant known as SNR G295.5+09.7, also nicknamed the Betta Fish Nebula for its resemblance to the chromatic betta fish. Nebulae are luminescent clouds of matter floating in the interstellar medium that are formed from gas, dust, and stellar material. This nebula may not have been imaged by a professional observatory before, making this image the first of its kind.

This image was taken with the 570-megapixel DOE-fabricated Dark Energy Camera (DECam), a high-performance imager mounted on the NSF Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO) in Chile, a Program of NSF NOIRLab. With its unparalleled wide-field imaging capabilities, DECam gives astronomers highly detailed views of nebulae and their surrounding cosmic environment.

As its technical name suggests, SNR G295.5+09.7 was formed by a supernova — the explosive death of a star many times more massive than our Sun. During the explosion, the star’s outer layers of material were expelled. The cast-off material expanded into the interstellar medium, crashing into the surrounding gas and causing it to glow, creating the blue ribbons we see today.

The rest of the massive star collapsed in on itself, unable to resist gravity. Total collapse was avoided through the formation of a neutron star, which sits in this image encircled by the outer shell of the nebula. Neutron stars are incredibly small and incredibly dense. They pack about 1.4 times the mass of our Sun into a sphere 20 kilometers (12 miles) in diameter. In fact, a whole neutron star could fit inside the city of Tucson, AZ, where NOIRLab Headquarters resides. If total collapse did occur, a black hole would have formed instead.

Zooming out, the Betta Fish Nebula is located in Centaurus, a constellation visible in the Southern Hemisphere, almost 6800 light-years away. It lies in the Carina–Sagittarius arm of our Milky Way Galaxy. In this image, thousands of stars from this arm rest in the background of the nebula. Hidden within the stellar multitude are galaxies outside of our own. Can you spot them in the zoomable version of this photo?

Additionally, the background of this nebula includes hazy, brown patches: interstellar clouds within our Milky Way. Interstellar clouds are similar to nebulae, but are vastly more dispersed regions. Our Solar System actually exists within one of these structures known as the Local Interstellar Cloud.

This image was taken as part of the NOIRLab Legacy Imaging Program — a continuation of the program started at the International Gemini Observatory in 2002, called the Gemini Legacy Imaging Program. Its aim is to use dedicated observing time on NOIRLab telescopes to acquire data specifically for color images to share with the public.

More information

The Dark Energy Camera (DECam) was designed specifically for the Dark Energy Survey (DES). It was funded by the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) and was built and tested at DOE's Fermilab.

NSF NOIRLab, the U.S. National Science Foundation center for ground-based optical-infrared astronomy, operates the International Gemini Observatory (a facility of NSF, NRC–Canada, ANID–Chile, MCTIC–Brazil, MINCyT–Argentina, and KASI–Republic of Korea), NSF Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO), NSF Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO), the Community Science and Data Center (CSDC), and NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory (in cooperation with DOE’s SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory). It is managed by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA) under a cooperative agreement with NSF and is headquartered in Tucson, Arizona. 

The scientific community is honored to have the opportunity to conduct astronomical research on I’oligam Du’ag (Kitt Peak) in Arizona, on Maunakea in Hawai‘i, and on Cerro Tololo and Cerro Pachón in Chile. We recognize and acknowledge the very significant cultural role and reverence of I’oligam Du’ag to the Tohono O’odham Nation, and Maunakea to the Kanaka Maoli (Native Hawaiians) community.
